conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. You're here tonight for your scheduled bronchoscopy with balloon dilation. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi doctor. I’m okay, a bit nervous. My breathing’s been a little worse since last time, but not bad right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your CT scan showed the trachea and bronchi are still narrowed from your polychondritis. The procedure tomorrow will help open them up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, like last time. I remember the dilation helped. But I’ve been seeing those lung spots on my scans—should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The new spots on your left lower lobe and right lung apex could be infection or inflammation. But you’re not running a fever or coughing more, so we don’t think it’s active. Infectious disease agrees—no antibiotics for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. But my white count is high again, right? It was 19.6 when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your white count is elevated, mostly neutrophils. But since you’re not sick-appearing and cultures show colonizing bacteria like Pseudomonas and Klebsiella, we believe this is from chronic airway inflammation, not a new infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the bacteria in my lungs are just… living there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They’re colonizers—common in patients with tracheostomies and chronic airway disease. Treating them wouldn’t help and might cause resistance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about after the procedure? Will I be in pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might have some soreness around the trach site. We’ll give oxycodone and acetaminophen as needed. Most patients say it feels like usual post-dilation discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The bronchoscopy went well—no complications. They dilated your trachea and main bronchi. You had some mucosal inflammation, but that’s expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My breathing feels about the same so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might take a day or two to notice improvement. We’ve started you on 50 mg of prednisone to reduce airway swelling, and you’ll taper it down over the next few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was only on 2.5 mg before. Is such a high dose safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a short course. We’re using it to calm the inflammation after the procedure. You’ll decrease by 10 mg every three days until you’re back to 7.5 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving—white count dropped to 13.3. You’re saturating well on 40% oxygen. We’re comfortable sending you home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep an eye on your breathing, fever, or increased secretions. Finish the prednisone taper, stay on your regular methotrexate and inhalers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see interventional pulmonology and rheumatology soon. We’ll also repeat a CBC to monitor your white count.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. Your breathing sounds stable, and your trach site looks good—just a little redness, no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take the prednisone as directed, use albuterol if short of breath, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I have my appointments lined up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll see you in follow-up. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. The team will get your discharge papers ready.
